raw_case_text:
A 66-year-old man presented and was admitted to the hospital with fever for 3 days and dyspnea for 1 day. The patient had been diagnosed with malignant pemphigus vulgaris and put on prednisolone, methylprednisolone and other immunosuppressive drugs for the past 9 years. On admission, he experienced respiratory failure. The absolute count of regulatory T lymphocytes was 156.67 cells/uL. The lactate dehydrogenase increased to 457 IU/L. The chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed multiple flaky, fuzzy, and high-density opacities in both lungs (Figure 1A). The patient had been on steroids for a long time. He had obvious hypoxia and had never had any other respiratory symptoms or other infections. On respiratory examination, the patient did not have many rales in the lungs. The lung CT scan showed interstitial changes. PCP, usually treated with sulfonamides, was considered a possible etiology because of his immunocompromised state. Caspofungin is a good treatment of choice for Aspergillus infection, which could not be excluded. For other atypical pathogens, moxifloxacin should be added. Thus he was given trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (3 tablets, twice daily for 3 weeks), caspofungin (loading dose, 70mg infused over 1 hour; maintenance dose, 50 mg daily infused over 1 hour for 2 weeks), steroids, and moxifloxacin. Consequently, his respiratory function improved, and his body temperature dropped. PCP was confirmed 4 days later when cysts were found in the sputum (Supplementary Material).
Curiously, the follow-up chest CT suggested an enlarged consolidation in the left upper lobe (Figure 1A-C). The patient was admitted to the hospital again due to cough, expectoration, and intermittent fever. Bronchoscopy was performed for 3 times. Smears and culture of the bronchial brush, tracheal secretions, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) were performed. Lung tissue was taken for culture and pathological examination, and tuberculosis was diagnosed (Figure 2). Antituberculosis treatment (isoniazid 300 mg once daily, rifapentine 600 mg twice weekly, ethambutol 750 mg once daily, and pyrazinamide 500 mg thrice daily) was given for 2 months and later ethambutol and pyrazinamide were excluded. Antituberculosis treatment lasted for 1 year. Simultaneously, traditional Chinese medicine techniques were used to manage the patient's psychological well-being and improve mental state. After 3 years of follow-up, the clinical outcome was good (Figure 3). The patient's complete course is shown in Figure 4.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old man on a 9-year regimen of corticosteroids and immunosuppressants for pemphigus vulgaris presented initially with a 3-day history of fever and 1-day history of dyspnea, and was later readmitted with recurrent cough, expectoration, and intermittent fever accompanied by an enlarging left upper lobe consolidation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Treated for the past 9 years with oral prednisolone, methylprednisolone, and other immunosuppressants for pemphigus vulgaris, the patient initially presented with 3 days of fever, 1 day of severe dyspnea, and hypoxemic respiratory failure. Following 4 days of empiric trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, caspofungin, moxifloxacin, and corticosteroids, sputum examination confirmed Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts and his fever and hypoxemia resolved. However, follow-up chest CT showed an enlarging consolidation in the left upper lobe, and he was readmitted with cough, sputum expectoration, and intermittent fever.
subjective.past_medical_history: Pemphigus vulgaris treated for 9 years with long-term prednisolone, methylprednisolone, and immunosuppressive therapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: First admission positive for 3 days of fever and 1 day of severe dyspnea; second admission positive for productive cough, expectoration, and intermittent fever. Home medications included long-term prednisolone, methylprednisolone, and immunosuppressants.

objective.physical_examination: First admission: Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure with scant pulmonary rales on chest auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: First admission laboratory test: Elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 457 IU/L.
objective.advanced_workup: First admission lymphocyte subsets, chest CT, and sputum microscopy: Absolute regulatory T-lymphocyte count 156.67 cells/μL; chest CT showed bilateral multiple flaky, hazy high-density and interstitial opacities; sputum microscopy on day 4 identified Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts. Readmission chest CT, serial bronchoscopies (3 times with bronchial brushings, tracheal secretions, and BALF), and lung biopsy: Follow-up chest CT showed an enlarging left upper lobe consolidation; lung tissue culture and histopathology confirmed active pulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis co-infection.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Sequential/concomitant opportunistic Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by sputum cyst identification on day 4) and left upper lobe pulmonary tuberculosis (confirmed by lung biopsy pathology and culture after three bronchoscopies) in a patient receiving 9 years of corticosteroid and immunosuppressive therapy for pemphigus vulgaris. Plan and clinical course: Initial PCP was successfully treated with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (3 tablets BID for 3 weeks), IV caspofungin (70 mg loading, 50 mg daily for 2 weeks), moxifloxacin, and corticosteroids. Upon confirmation of left upper lobe pulmonary tuberculosis, he completed a 1-year antituberculosis regimen (2 months of intensive isoniazid 300 mg QD, rifapentine 600 mg twice weekly, ethambutol 750 mg QD, and pyrazinamide 500 mg TID, followed by 10 months of isoniazid and rifapentine) plus supportive traditional Chinese medicine, achieving a favorable clinical and radiographic outcome at 3-year follow-up.
